specStatements.text: Life cycle assessments (LCAs) are carried out to assess the environmental impact of products in each of these stages:
use and operation during its lifetime
disposal at the end of its useful life, including transport and distribution at each stage.

Use of water, resources, energy sources and production of some wastes can be fairly easily quantified. Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects is less straightforward and requires value judgements, so LCA is not a purely objective process.
Selective or abbreviated LCAs can be devised to evaluate a product but these can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions, eg in support of claims for advertising purposes.
Students should be able to carry out simple comparative LCAs for shopping bags made from plastic and paper.
The reduction in use, reuse and recycling of materials by end users reduces the use of limited resources, use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts.

Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are produced from limited raw materials. Much of the energy for the processes comes from limited resources. Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying and mining causes environmental impacts.
Some products, such as glass bottles, can be reused. Glass bottles can be crushed and melted to make different glass products. Other products cannot be reused and so are recycled for a different use.

Metals can be recycled by melting and recasting or reforming into different products. The amount of separation required for recycling depends on the material and the properties required of the final product. For example, some scrap steel can be added to iron from a blast furnace to reduce the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore.
Students should be able to evaluate ways of reducing the use of limited resources, given appropriate information.

concepts.term: Life cycle assessment (LCA)
concepts.definition: An assessment carried out to judge the environmental impact of a product in each of four stages: extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation during its lifetime; and disposal at the end of its useful life, including transport and distribution at each stage.

concepts.term: Stage 1: extracting and processing raw materials
concepts.definition: The first stage assessed in an LCA. It covers obtaining the raw material from the Earth or from living things and every process needed to turn it into a usable material, for example mining an ore and reducing it to the metal, or drilling for crude oil and processing it into a polymer.

concepts.term: Stage 2: manufacturing and packaging
concepts.definition: The second stage assessed in an LCA. It covers making the product itself from the processed material and also producing the packaging the product is sold or transported in.

concepts.term: Stage 3: use and operation during its lifetime
concepts.definition: The third stage assessed in an LCA. It covers the impact of the product while it is in use, for example the electricity and water a washing machine uses, or the detergents needed to wash a bottle that is refilled.

concepts.term: Stage 4: disposal at the end of its useful life
concepts.definition: The fourth stage assessed in an LCA. It covers what happens once the product is no longer wanted, for example collection, landfill, incineration, or collection and processing for recycling.

concepts.term: Transport and distribution in an LCA
concepts.definition: Moving materials, parts and finished products around is not a separate stage of an LCA. It is included at each stage, so the impact of transport and distribution is counted from raw material to final disposal.

concepts.term: Quantities that are fairly easily quantified
concepts.definition: Use of water, use of resources, use of energy sources and production of some wastes can be fairly easily quantified in an LCA, because they can be measured or calculated as amounts.

concepts.term: Value judgement in an LCA
concepts.definition: A decision about how much importance to give to something, made by the person carrying out the assessment rather than by measurement. Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects is less straightforward than measuring water or energy use and requires value judgements.

concepts.term: LCA is not a purely objective process
concepts.definition: Because value judgements are needed to put numbers on pollutant effects, two people assessing the same product can reach different conclusions. An LCA is therefore not purely objective, even though parts of it rest on measured data.

concepts.term: Selective or abbreviated LCA
concepts.definition: A shortened assessment that looks at only some stages of a product's life, or only some of the impacts. Selective or abbreviated LCAs can be devised to evaluate a product, but leaving parts out changes the conclusion that is reached.

concepts.term: Misuse of LCAs to reach pre-determined conclusions
concepts.definition: A selective or abbreviated LCA can be misused by choosing in advance the conclusion that is wanted and then including only the stages or impacts that support it, for example in support of claims made for advertising purposes.

concepts.term: Comparative LCA of plastic and paper shopping bags
concepts.definition: A simple side-by-side assessment of two products across the same four stages. For plastic and paper bags this means comparing raw materials (crude oil against wood), the energy and water used in manufacture, how many times each bag is used, and what happens to each bag at disposal.

concepts.term: Reduction in use, reuse and recycling by end users
concepts.definition: Three distinct actions taken by the people who use products. All three reduce the use of limited resources, the use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts. Reduction in use means needing fewer products; reuse means using the same product again; recycling means processing a material into something new.

concepts.term: Limited raw materials
concepts.definition: Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are produced from limited raw materials, and much of the energy for the processes also comes from limited resources.

concepts.term: Environmental impacts of quarrying and mining
concepts.definition: Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying and mining causes environmental impacts, such as damage to the landscape and habitats, noise and dust, and the waste rock and other wastes produced.

concepts.term: Reuse
concepts.definition: Using a product again in the form it already has. Some products, such as glass bottles, can be reused, for example by washing and refilling them.

concepts.term: Recycling for a different use
concepts.definition: Processing a material so that it can be made into something new. Glass bottles can be crushed and melted to make different glass products, and products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use.

concepts.term: Recycling metals
concepts.definition: Metals can be recycled by melting them and then recasting or reforming them into different products.

concepts.term: Separation required for recycling
concepts.definition: The amount of separation required before a material is recycled depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product. A product that must have a precise composition needs more careful separation than one that does not.

concepts.term: Scrap steel added to iron from a blast furnace
concepts.definition: Some scrap steel can be added to iron from a blast furnace. This reduces the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore, so less ore is mined and less ore has to be reduced.

concepts.term: Evaluating ways of reducing the use of limited resources
concepts.definition: Weighing up the benefits and drawbacks of an option using the information given, rather than assuming one option is always best. An evaluation considers the resources, energy and water used, the waste produced and the environmental impacts, and reaches a supported conclusion.

misconceptions.question: Which parts of a product's life does an LCA assess?
misconceptions.correct: An LCA assesses all four stages: extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use and operation during its lifetime, and disposal at the end of its useful life, including transport and distribution at each stage.
misconceptions.misconception: An LCA is about how a product is made, so it only looks at the factory.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Manufacture is the stage students picture most easily, and it is the stage most often shown in textbook images and adverts. The word 'production' is also used loosely in everyday speech to mean the whole life of a product.
misconceptions.correction: Manufacturing and packaging is only one of the four stages. A product with a clean factory can still have a large overall impact from raw material extraction, from its use, or from its disposal.

misconceptions.question: What does the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage include?
misconceptions.correct: It includes both obtaining the raw material and every process needed to turn it into a usable material, such as reducing an ore to a metal or converting crude oil into a polymer.
misconceptions.misconception: Extracting raw materials just means digging them out of the ground; turning them into a material is part of manufacturing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'extracting' is the one students notice, and 'processing' in the same phrase is skimmed over. Extraction of metals is also taught as its own topic, which makes it feel separate.
misconceptions.correction: The stage is named 'extracting and processing raw materials'. Both halves belong to stage 1, so smelting an ore or cracking a fraction of crude oil is counted here, not under manufacturing.

misconceptions.question: Is packaging included in a life cycle assessment?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The second stage is 'manufacturing and packaging', so producing the packaging is assessed alongside making the product itself.
misconceptions.misconception: Packaging is thrown straight away and is not the actual product, so it does not count in the LCA.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of the LCA as being about the product, and packaging feels like a temporary extra rather than something that itself had to be made from raw materials.
misconceptions.correction: Packaging is made from raw materials, uses energy to manufacture and creates waste at disposal. The specification names it in the same stage as manufacturing, so it must be included.

misconceptions.question: Does every product have an impact during the 'use and operation' stage?
misconceptions.correct: The use stage is assessed for every product, although its size varies. A washing machine uses electricity and water; a shopping bag or a refilled bottle has impacts from washing, or from how many times it can be used before it fails.
misconceptions.misconception: Only products that are plugged in have a use stage; things like bags and bottles have no impact once you own them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy labels on appliances make the use stage very visible for electrical goods, so students assume the stage means 'energy used while switched on'.
misconceptions.correction: 'Use and operation during its lifetime' covers whatever the product consumes or causes while it is being used, including water and detergent for washing a reusable item, and how long it lasts before replacement.

misconceptions.question: Does a product that is recycled still have a disposal stage in its LCA?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Collecting, sorting and processing the material at the end of its useful life all have impacts and are assessed in the disposal stage, along with the transport involved.
misconceptions.misconception: If something is recycled it has not been thrown away, so there is no disposal impact at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is presented as the environmentally good choice, so students treat it as having zero impact rather than as having a smaller impact than landfill.
misconceptions.correction: Recycling is a route for the product at the end of its useful life, not an escape from that stage. Lorries, sorting plants and remelting all use energy, so the impact is reduced rather than removed.

misconceptions.question: How is transport treated in a life cycle assessment?
misconceptions.correct: Transport and distribution are included at each stage of the life cycle, not counted once in a stage of their own.
misconceptions.misconception: Transport is a fifth stage of the LCA, added on after disposal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Transport is listed at the end of the specification's list of stages, so it reads like another item on the list rather than a note about all of them.
misconceptions.correction: The wording is 'including transport and distribution at each stage'. Moving ore to a smelter, parts to a factory, goods to shops and waste to a tip are each counted within their own stage.

misconceptions.question: Does an LCA give one definite answer about which product is better?
misconceptions.correct: No. Because allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires value judgements, LCA is not a purely objective process and different assessors can reach different conclusions from the same product.
misconceptions.misconception: An LCA is a scientific calculation, so it produces one correct score and any two assessments should agree.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate anything with numbers in it with objectivity, and the phrase 'assessment' sounds like a measurement rather than a judgement.
misconceptions.correction: Parts of an LCA are measured, but the weighting given to different pollutant effects is a judgement. Disagreement between two LCAs does not automatically mean one contains an arithmetic mistake.

misconceptions.question: Which parts of an LCA can be quantified fairly easily?
misconceptions.correct: Use of water, resources and energy sources, and production of some wastes, can be fairly easily quantified. Putting numerical values on pollutant effects is less straightforward.
misconceptions.misconception: Everything in an LCA can be measured; the harm a pollutant does is just another number you look up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Data tables in exam questions give figures for pollutant emissions, so students assume the harm caused is equally measurable. Emissions can be measured; the damage they do must be valued.
misconceptions.correction: The mass of a pollutant released can be measured, but deciding how much weight to give that harm compared with, say, water use is a value judgement, which is why LCA is not purely objective.

misconceptions.question: Is a selective or abbreviated LCA as trustworthy as a full one?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Selective or abbreviated LCAs can be devised to evaluate a product, but because they leave stages or impacts out they can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions.
misconceptions.misconception: A shortened LCA is just a quicker version using the same data, so it must reach the same conclusion.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of a summary as a shorter account of the same thing, rather than as a selection that can change what the account shows.
misconceptions.correction: Leaving out a stage removes its impacts from the total. An assessment covering only manufacturing can make a product look far better than a full assessment would.

misconceptions.question: Should an environmental claim in an advert be accepted because it is based on an LCA?
misconceptions.correct: No. The specification states that LCAs can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions, for example in support of claims for advertising purposes, so the basis of the claim should be checked.
misconceptions.misconception: The claim quotes an LCA, and LCAs are scientific, so the claim must be true.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Attaching the word 'scientific' or 'proven' to a claim gives it authority, and students are not used to asking which stages a published figure covered.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what the LCA included: which stages, which impacts, and who paid for it. A company has an interest in the conclusion, and a selective LCA can be built to support it.

misconceptions.question: Which is better for the environment, a paper shopping bag or a plastic one?
misconceptions.correct: It depends on the figures for each stage and on how many times each bag is used. A comparative LCA has to be carried out; neither material is automatically better.
misconceptions.misconception: Paper bags are always better than plastic bags because paper comes from trees and plastic does not rot.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Campaigns against plastic waste make plastic the obvious villain, and the visible litter problem is easier to picture than the energy and water used to make paper.
misconceptions.correction: Making a paper bag typically uses more energy and water per bag, while a plastic bag is lighter and can often be used many more times. The comparison must cover all four stages before a conclusion is drawn.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter how many times a shopping bag is used when comparing bags?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Comparing the impacts per use, taking account of how many times each bag is used, is central to a fair comparative LCA of plastic and paper bags.
misconceptions.misconception: An LCA compares how the bags are made, so how often you use them afterwards is not part of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students focus on the manufacturing figures given in the data table and treat 'one bag' as the fair unit of comparison, without noticing that the two bags do different amounts of work.
misconceptions.correction: Use and operation during its lifetime is one of the four stages. A bag used 20 times spreads its manufacturing impact over 20 uses, so impact per use, not per bag, is the fair comparison.

misconceptions.question: Are reduction in use, reuse and recycling the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: They are three different actions. Reduction in use means using fewer products; reuse means using the same product again as it is; recycling means processing the material into something new. All three reduce the use of limited resources, energy, waste and environmental impacts.
misconceptions.misconception: They all mean 'being green', so any of the three words can be used for any action that keeps something out of landfill.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three words appear together as a slogan, which blurs the differences between them, and 'recycling' is used loosely in everyday speech for putting anything in a green bin.
misconceptions.correction: Check what happens to the object. Refilling a bottle is reuse; crushing and melting it is recycling; buying one large bottle instead of six small ones is reduction in use.

misconceptions.question: Does recycling a material use energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Collecting, sorting, melting and reforming a material all use energy, and much of that energy comes from limited resources. Recycling reduces the use of energy sources compared with making the material from new raw materials; it does not remove it.
misconceptions.misconception: Recycled products are made from waste, so making them uses no energy or resources.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is taught as the solution to resource use, so students slide from 'uses less' to 'uses none'. The energy costs of collection and remelting are invisible to the end user.
misconceptions.correction: Compare, do not zero. Recycling aluminium uses far less energy than extracting it by electrolysis, but lorries, sorting plants and furnaces still consume energy from limited resources.

misconceptions.question: Which everyday materials come from limited raw materials?
misconceptions.correct: Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are all produced from limited raw materials.
misconceptions.misconception: Only plastics and fuels are limited; there is so much rock and sand in the Earth that metals, glass and bricks can never run out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Running out' is taught most often about crude oil, and rock appears endlessly abundant. Students confuse how much of an element exists with how much is available in ore rich enough to be worth extracting.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics together as coming from limited raw materials. Useful ore and suitable sand are finite, and the easiest deposits are used first.

misconceptions.question: Is crushing and melting a glass bottle to make a jar an example of reuse?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is recycling. The bottle no longer exists as a bottle; the glass has been processed into a different glass product. Reuse would be washing the same bottle and filling it again.
misconceptions.misconception: The same glass is being used a second time, so it counts as reuse.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both words contain the idea of 'using again', and students apply reuse to the material rather than to the object.
misconceptions.correction: Reuse keeps the object intact and uses it again for a purpose; recycling destroys the object and processes the material into something new. The specification gives both routes for glass bottles.

misconceptions.question: Must a recycled material be made back into the same product?
misconceptions.correct: No. Products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use, and glass bottles can be crushed and melted to make different glass products.
misconceptions.misconception: Recycling means turning something back into what it was, so recycled bottles must become bottles again.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The recycling symbol suggests a closed loop, and the simplest classroom examples show a material returning to its original form.
misconceptions.correction: Recycled material is made into whatever product its properties and purity allow. This is why the amount of separation needed depends on the properties required of the final product.

misconceptions.question: Do metals always have to be fully separated before they are recycled?
misconceptions.correct: No. The amount of separation required depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product.
misconceptions.misconception: Any mixture would spoil the metal, so scrap has to be sorted into completely pure single metals before melting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the rule that impurities weaken or contaminate a substance, learned in purity and separation work, to every recycling situation.
misconceptions.correction: Where the final product needs a precise composition, careful separation is required; where it does not, mixed scrap can be melted together. Scrap steel added to a blast furnace does not need the same sorting as scrap for a high-specification alloy.

misconceptions.question: What does adding scrap steel to iron from a blast furnace achieve?
misconceptions.correct: It reduces the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore, so less ore has to be mined and reduced.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding scrap steel means no iron ore is needed at all, because the furnace is running on recycled metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'reduce the amount' as 'remove the need for'. The wording that scrap is added to iron from a blast furnace is also skimmed, so the ore route is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: The scrap is added to iron that has already come from the blast furnace, so ore is still being used. The benefit is that less iron has to be extracted from ore than would otherwise be needed.

misconceptions.question: What environmental impacts does quarrying and mining cause?
misconceptions.correct: Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying and mining causes environmental impacts, including damage to land and habitats, noise and dust, and large amounts of waste rock.
misconceptions.misconception: Mining and quarrying only spoil the view; once the site is landscaped there is no impact left.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The visual scar of a quarry is the impact students can see in a photograph, so it stands in for all the others.
misconceptions.correction: Appearance is one impact among several. Habitats are destroyed, waste rock and dust are produced, and the processes consume energy from limited resources.

misconceptions.question: Is only the raw material limited when a material such as glass or metal is produced?
misconceptions.correct: No. The raw materials are limited and, in addition, much of the energy for the processes comes from limited resources.
misconceptions.misconception: The ore or sand is the limited part; the energy for heating and melting is just electricity, which we can always make more of.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electricity arrives at a socket with no visible fuel, so students separate it from the fossil fuels that generate much of it.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that much of the energy for these processes comes from limited resources. Reducing the energy used, for example by recycling rather than extracting, conserves those resources too.

mcqs.stem: A life cycle assessment of a product assesses its environmental impact in which stages?

options.text: Manufacturing and packaging only, because that is the stage that uses the most energy
options.rationale: Students who picture an LCA as an assessment of a factory choose the manufacturing stage alone.

options.text: Extraction, manufacture, use and disposal, with transport assessed as a separate stage
options.rationale: Transport is read as a fifth item on the list rather than as something counted at every stage.

options.text: Extracting the raw materials and disposal, because these are the two polluting stages
options.rationale: Mining and landfill are the most visible impacts, so a student drops the two middle stages.

options.text: Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, disposal
options.rationale: These are the four stages named in the specification, with transport and distribution included at each of them.

mcqs.stem: Why does a manufacturer carry out a life cycle assessment on a new product?

options.text: To work out the profit that will be made from selling the product
options.rationale: The word 'assessment' is read as a business appraisal rather than an environmental one.

options.text: To measure the pollution released by the factory where it is made
options.rationale: Reduces the LCA to the manufacturing stage, which is the stage students picture first.

options.text: To produce one objective score that ranks the product against all others
options.rationale: Treats the LCA as a purely objective calculation rather than one requiring value judgements.

options.text: To assess the environmental impact of the product at every stage of its life
options.rationale: This is the purpose given in the specification: to assess environmental impact in each of the four stages.

mcqs.stem: A poly(ethene) carrier bag is made from crude oil. Which of these belongs to the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage of its LCA?

options.text: Wrapping the finished bags into bundles to be sent out to the shops
options.rationale: Packaging is either ignored altogether or attached to the wrong stage.

options.text: Only the drilling of the crude oil, because processing is a later stage
options.rationale: The student reads 'extracting' and overlooks 'and processing' in the same stage.

options.text: Drilling for crude oil and cracking a fraction of it to obtain ethene
options.rationale: Both obtaining the raw material and processing it into a usable material fall in stage 1.

options.text: Collecting used bags from households so that they can be sorted out
options.rationale: Collection at the end of life is disposal, but students group anything involving the raw material's fate together.

mcqs.stem: Finished paper bags are put into cardboard boxes at the factory before being sent to shops. In an LCA of the paper bags, this belongs to:

options.text: no stage at all, because packaging is thrown away and is not the product
options.rationale: Packaging feels like a temporary extra rather than something made from raw materials.

options.text: manufacturing and packaging, with the transport counted at that same stage
options.rationale: Producing packaging sits in stage 2, and transport and distribution are included at each stage.

options.text: a separate transport stage, which is added on after the disposal stage
options.rationale: Transport is treated as a fifth stage instead of being counted within each stage.

options.text: use and operation, because the boxes are used by the shop receiving them
options.rationale: The word 'use' is applied to whoever handles the item rather than to the product's working life.

mcqs.stem: A glass milk bottle is washed and refilled every week. Which of these belongs to the 'use and operation during its lifetime' stage of its LCA?

options.text: The energy used to melt the sand and shape the bottle at the works
options.rationale: Manufacturing energy is easily confused with the energy consumed while a product is in use.

options.text: Nothing, because a bottle is not powered and so has no use stage
options.rationale: The use stage is taken to mean electricity consumed, so an unpowered product seems to have none.

options.text: The water and the energy used to wash the bottle before refilling
options.rationale: What a product consumes each time it is used is exactly the use and operation stage.

options.text: The energy used to melt the glass down when the bottle is finished
options.rationale: End-of-life processing is disposal; students who blur the stages group all energy use together.

mcqs.stem: An empty steel food can is put out for kerbside recycling collection. In an LCA of the can, the impact of this is:

options.text: zero, because a can that is sent off for recycling is never disposed of
options.rationale: Recycling is treated as having no impact rather than a reduced impact.

options.text: counted only within a separate stage covering all transport of the can
options.rationale: Transport is again pulled out into a stage of its own.

options.text: part of the disposal stage, including transporting the collected cans
options.rationale: Recycling is a route at the end of the can's useful life, and transport is counted at that stage.

options.text: part of the manufacturing stage, because the metal will be melted again
options.rationale: Melting is associated with making things, so the student files it under manufacture.

mcqs.stem: How are transport and distribution treated in a life cycle assessment?

options.text: They are included at each stage of the life cycle
options.rationale: The specification says 'including transport and distribution at each stage'.

options.text: They form a fifth stage, placed after final disposal
options.rationale: The phrase appears at the end of the list, so it reads as another list item.

options.text: They are counted only when raw materials are moved
options.rationale: Ore lorries are the transport image students hold, so they limit it to stage 1.

options.text: They are left out, because they are hard to measure
options.rationale: Anything outside the factory is assumed to fall outside the assessment.

mcqs.stem: Which of these can be quantified fairly easily in a life cycle assessment?

options.text: The value that society places on protecting a nearby woodland
options.rationale: Plausible as an LCA input, but it is a judgement rather than a measurable quantity.

options.text: The harm done to a river by a pollutant released from the works
options.rationale: Emissions can be measured, so students assume the harm they cause can be too.

options.text: The overall objective score showing which of two products is best
options.rationale: Assumes an LCA delivers a single objective figure.

options.text: The volume of water used and the waste produced in manufacture
options.rationale: Use of water, resources, energy sources and production of some wastes can be fairly easily quantified.

mcqs.stem: Why is a life cycle assessment not a purely objective process?

options.text: Different scientists choose different stages of a product's life
options.rationale: The four stages are fixed by the method; it is the weighting of impacts that varies.

options.text: Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires judgements
options.rationale: This is the reason given in the specification for LCA not being purely objective.

options.text: Water use, energy use and waste produced cannot be measured at all
options.rationale: Overcorrects: these are the parts the specification says are fairly easily quantified.

options.text: Two assessments of one product can never produce the same figures
options.rationale: Turns 'not purely objective' into 'entirely unreliable', which overstates the point.

mcqs.stem: A drinks company publishes an LCA of its bottle that covers the manufacturing stage only. Why is this a problem?

options.text: An abbreviated LCA uses the same data, so it gives the same result
options.rationale: A shortened account is assumed to be a summary rather than a selection.

options.text: An LCA is scientific, so a conclusion drawn from it must be correct
options.rationale: Scientific method is taken as a guarantee of the conclusion reached.

options.text: A selective LCA can be used to reach a conclusion decided in advance
options.rationale: The specification warns that selective or abbreviated LCAs can be misused to reach pre-determined conclusions.

options.text: Manufacturing has no environmental impact that is worth reporting
options.rationale: Inverts the problem: the objection is what was left out, not what was included.

mcqs.stem: An advert states that a paper cup is 'proven by science to be the greenest choice'. What is the best response to this claim?

options.text: The claim must be true, because an LCA is a scientific process
options.rationale: The authority of the word 'science' is accepted without asking what was assessed.

options.text: The LCA behind the claim may be selective and should be checked
options.rationale: LCAs can be misused in support of claims for advertising purposes, so the basis of the claim must be examined.

options.text: Paper products are always better, so the claim needs no checking
options.rationale: The belief that paper beats plastic makes the student accept the conclusion.

options.text: No LCA can ever support a claim made for advertising purposes
options.rationale: Overcorrects: the specification warns of misuse, not that every advertised LCA is false.

mcqs.stem: In a simple comparative LCA of plastic and paper shopping bags, which comparison is the fairest?

options.text: The impact per use, taking account of how often each bag is used
options.rationale: The two bags last different lengths of time, so impact per use is the fair basis for comparison.

options.text: The cost of each bag to the shop, since price reflects resource use
options.rationale: Cost is a familiar proxy, but it reflects markets rather than environmental impact.

options.text: The impact of making one bag, since reuse is not a part of an LCA
options.rationale: Ignores the use stage and compares one bag with one bag.

options.text: Whether the bag is paper, since paper is the greener material used
options.rationale: Substitutes a blanket belief about materials for the actual assessment.

mcqs.stem: Making a paper bag needs 4 times as much energy as making a plastic bag. On average a plastic bag is used 20 times and a paper bag 3 times. Which conclusion follows from these figures?

options.text: The paper bag is better, because paper is the more natural material
options.rationale: The student ignores the figures and falls back on a belief about the materials.

options.text: Per use, the paper bag needs more energy than the plastic bag does
options.rationale: Taking one unit of energy per plastic bag: plastic is 1/20 per use, paper is 4/3 per use, so paper is higher.

options.text: The two bags are equal, since the number of uses is not counted
options.rationale: Discards the use stage, so only the manufacturing figures are compared.

options.text: Per use, the plastic bag needs four times the energy of the paper
options.rationale: The ratio is read the wrong way round and the number of uses is not applied.

mcqs.stem: Reduction in use, reuse and recycling of materials by end users reduces:

options.text: waste only, because recycling a material uses no energy of its own
options.rationale: Recycling is treated as having zero energy cost, so only waste appears to fall.

options.text: the price of the products, but not the quantity of raw material used
options.rationale: Confuses an economic saving with a saving of resources.

options.text: waste and energy use, but only for reuse rather than for recycling
options.rationale: Separates the three actions and assumes they do not have the same benefits.

options.text: use of limited resources, use of energy sources, waste and impacts
options.rationale: These are the four things the specification says all three actions reduce.

mcqs.stem: A family have the same glass bottle washed and refilled with milk each week. This is an example of:

options.text: recycling, because the bottle is kept out of landfill waste
options.rationale: 'Recycling' is used loosely for anything that avoids being thrown away.

options.text: reduction in use, because fewer bottles are melted down
options.rationale: The three terms are treated as interchangeable labels for green behaviour.

options.text: disposal, because the bottle will be thrown away one day
options.rationale: Focuses on the eventual end of life rather than on what is happening now.

options.text: reuse, because the bottle itself is used again as a bottle
options.rationale: The object stays intact and is used again for the same purpose, which is reuse.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the materials used to make everyday products is correct?

options.text: Only plastics are limited, because metal ores can always be mined
options.rationale: 'Running out' is associated with crude oil alone, and rock looks abundant.

options.text: All of the energy for making these materials comes from unlimited sources
options.rationale: Electricity at a socket hides the limited resources used to generate much of it.

options.text: Metals, glass, ceramics and most plastics come from limited materials
options.rationale: The specification lists metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics together.

options.text: Clay ceramics are limited, but glass and metals can be remade freely
options.rationale: Splits the list arbitrarily; recyclability is confused with an unlimited supply.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an environmental impact of obtaining raw materials by quarrying and mining?

options.text: Habitats are destroyed and waste rock and dust are produced on site
options.rationale: Quarrying and mining damage land and habitats and generate large amounts of waste rock and dust.

options.text: The only effect is that the landscape is left looking less attractive
options.rationale: The visible scar in a photograph stands in for all the other impacts.

options.text: There is no lasting impact, since the Earth's supply is unlimited
options.rationale: Belief in an endless supply removes any reason to count an impact.

options.text: The ore that is left behind holds a lower percentage of metal
options.rationale: A real consequence of mining the richest deposits first, but an economic one rather than an environmental impact.

mcqs.stem: Used glass bottles are collected, crushed and melted to make glass jars. This is best described as:

options.text: recycling, because the glass is processed into a new product
options.rationale: The bottle is destroyed and the glass is made into a different glass product, which is recycling.

options.text: reuse, because the same glass is being used a second time
options.rationale: 'Reuse' is applied to the material rather than to the object.

options.text: reduction in use, because fewer new jars need to be bought
options.rationale: Confuses the three end-user actions; nothing here reduces the number of products used.

options.text: impossible, because glass can only be remade into bottles
options.rationale: Assumes recycling must return a material to its original product.

mcqs.stem: What is the difference between reusing a glass bottle and recycling it?

options.text: There is no difference; crushing and melting glass counts as reuse
options.rationale: The two terms are collapsed into one because both involve using glass again.

options.text: Recycling means the melted glass has to be made into bottles again
options.rationale: Recycling is pictured as a closed loop back to the original product.

options.text: Reusing keeps the bottle whole; recycling melts it into new glass
options.rationale: Reuse uses the object again as it is; recycling processes the material into a different product.

options.text: Reusing means the bottle goes to landfill after one further use
options.rationale: Adds a limit that is not there; a reused bottle can be refilled many times.

mcqs.stem: How are metals recycled?

options.text: They are heated with carbon to reduce them back into the metal
options.rationale: Imports the extraction method for the metal from its ore into recycling.

options.text: They are melted and then recast or reformed into new products
options.rationale: This is the method given in the specification for recycling metals.

options.text: They must first be separated into completely pure single metals
options.rationale: The purity rule from separation techniques is applied to all recycling.

options.text: They are cleaned and reshaped without any energy being required
options.rationale: Recycling is assumed to have no energy cost at all.

mcqs.stem: How much separation of scrap metal is needed before it is recycled?

options.text: It depends on the material and the properties the product needs
options.rationale: The specification states that the amount of separation required depends on both of these.

options.text: Complete separation is always required before any metal is melted
options.rationale: Assumes any mixture would ruin the recycled metal.

options.text: None is ever needed, because melting removes all the other metals
options.rationale: Melting is imagined to purify the metal, as boiling purifies water.

options.text: It depends only on how much scrap a blast furnace is able to take
options.rationale: Generalises the single blast furnace example to all metal recycling.

mcqs.stem: Why is some scrap steel added to iron from a blast furnace?

options.text: It cuts the amount of iron that must be extracted from iron ore
options.rationale: This is exactly the reason given in the specification for adding scrap steel.

options.text: It removes the need for any iron ore to be used in the process
options.rationale: 'Reduce the amount' is read as 'remove the need for'.

options.text: It lets the scrap be used without separating any of it beforehand
options.rationale: Mixes up the separation point with the reason for adding scrap at all.

options.text: It makes the iron ore easier to reduce inside the blast furnace
options.rationale: Invents a chemical effect on the reduction of the ore that the specification does not give.

mcqs.stem: A town council wants to reduce the use of limited resources. Which action would achieve this?

options.text: Sending household waste to landfill rather than to an incinerator
options.rationale: Changes the disposal route but does nothing to reduce the resources used in the first place.

options.text: Setting up a scheme to collect and refill glass milk bottles
options.rationale: Reuse by end users reduces the use of limited resources, energy sources, waste and impacts.

options.text: Switching to newly made plastic bottles, as plastic is unlimited
options.rationale: Rests on the belief that only some materials come from limited raw materials.

options.text: Adding more iron ore to the blast furnace in place of scrap steel
options.rationale: Reverses the benefit of scrap steel, which is that less iron is extracted from ore.

mcqs.stem: A council compares two ways of supplying drinks: refillable glass bottles that are collected and washed, or cans made from recycled aluminium. Which point belongs in a fair evaluation?

options.text: Recycling the cans uses no energy, so this option has no impact
options.rationale: Recycling is credited with a zero energy cost rather than a reduced one.

options.text: Refilling a bottle counts as recycling, so the options are equal
options.rationale: Reuse and recycling are treated as the same action, so no comparison is made.

options.text: Only the cost to the council matters when resources are limited
options.rationale: Substitutes an economic test for an environmental one.

options.text: Washing the bottles uses water and energy, which must be weighed
options.rationale: The use stage of a reusable bottle has real impacts, and an evaluation must weigh them against the benefits.
